Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(Entertainment Weekly) -- J.J. Abrams' franchise reboot boldly went where no Star Trek movie has gone before, grossing a stellar $72.5 million from Friday through Sunday, according to early estimates by Hollywood.com Box Office. In the film, Spock (Zachary Quinto, left) and Kirk get off on the wrong foot. That's the second-best opening of 2009 (after X-Men Origins: Wolverine's $85.1 million last weekend), and it includes a whopping $8.2 million earned in IMAX showings, a new one-weekend record for the large format (beating The Dark Knight's $6.3 million). What's more, if you add in the $4 million that the movie starring Chris Pine and Zachary Quinto earned in late-Thursday showings, Star Trek has banked an impressive $76.5 million so far -- well ahead of most expectations. This result is highly logical. Considering all the hype and buzz and strong reviews that Star Trek has garnered, it's no surprise that this film's opening sum is by far the biggest of any Star Trek movie: Of the 10 previous flicks in the franchise, 1996's Star Trek: First Contact bowed best, with (only) $30.7 million over three days. Moreover, a look at the movie's CinemaScore report card reveals some potentially good news. While it drew an expected crowd mostly comprised of older males, Star Trek's solid-A grade shows that word of mouth could be strong enough to bring in fans outside of the franchise's usual demographic (i.e. people who weren't alive in the 1980s...and women) as the weeks go on. Unless said folks are too distracted by Angels & Demons, Night at the Museum 2, and all the other big flicks on tap, of course. X-Men Origins: Wolverine (No. 2) was next with $27 million on a 68 percent decline. Fanboy-driven films always fall hard, but this drop is particularly hefty. Nevertheless, Hugh Jackman's franchise flick has already banked $129.6 million in 10 days. Fellow holdovers Ghosts of Girlfriends Past (No. 3 with $10.5 million), Obsessed (No. 4 with $6.6 million), and 17 Again (No. 5 with $4.4 million) rounded out the top five. And the comedy Next Day Air failed to take off, grossing just $4 million at No. 6. And in limited release, neither Rudo y Cursi nor Little Ashes made much of a mark, as each averaged well under $7,000 per theater. Overall, the box office was up nearly 22 percent from the same frame a year ago (when the infamous Speed Racer hit a bump in the road). # Star Trek Reboot Warps Past Box Office Expectations

(Entertainment Weekly) -- The Star Trek franchise achieved unprecedented success this weekend, with J.J. Abrams' reimagined take on the sci-fi classic pulling in a remarkable $72.5 million over the Friday-to-Sunday period, based on preliminary figures from Hollywood.com Box Office. The film follows a rocky relationship between Kirk and Spock (played by Zachary Quinto).

This ranks as 2009's second-strongest debut, trailing only X-Men Origins: Wolverine's $85.1 million from the previous week. Notably, IMAX screenings alone contributed $8.2 million to the total—shattering the previous single-weekend IMAX benchmark of $6.3 million set by The Dark Knight. When factoring in the additional $4 million generated from Thursday night preview screenings, the Chris Pine and Zachary Quinto vehicle has already accumulated $76.5 million, surpassing most industry predictions.

None of this comes as a shock, really. Given the enthusiastic buzz and glowing critical reception surrounding the film, its record-breaking opening makes perfect sense—it now stands as the highest-grossing debut in the franchise's history. For comparison, the previous champion among the series' ten earlier installments was 1996's Star Trek: First Contact, which managed just $30.7 million in its opening weekend.

Additional encouraging signs come from the film's CinemaScore rating. Though the initial audience skewed toward older male viewers—the franchise's traditional base—the impressive A grade suggests positive word-of-mouth could expand the film's reach to non-traditional Trek fans (think: women, and anyone born after the 1980s) in coming weeks. That is, assuming these potential new viewers aren't lured away by competing releases like Angels & Demons or Night at the Museum 2.

Meanwhile, X-Men Origins: Wolverine slipped to second place with $27 million, representing a steep 68 percent drop-off. While comic-book adaptations typically experience significant second-weekend declines, this fall was notably steeper than usual. Still, Hugh Jackman's mutant saga has amassed a healthy $129.6 million after just ten days in theaters.

Rounding out the top five were returning titles Ghosts of Girlfriends Past (third place, $10.5 million), Obsessed (fourth, $6.6 million), and 17 Again (fifth, $4.4 million). Meanwhile, the comedy Next Day Air struggled to gain traction, earning only $4 million and landing at sixth place.

Limited releases fared poorly this weekend as well—both Rudo y Cursi and Little Ashes underperformed, with per-theater averages falling well below $7,000.

Overall industry revenue climbed approximately 22 percent compared to the same weekend last year, when Speed Racer notoriously stalled at the box office. Not a bad Mother's Day present for the film industry, all things considered—Happy Mother's Day to all the moms out there!

J.J. Abrams' highly anticipated reimagining of the *Star Trek* franchise has boldly gone where few 2009 releases have gone before, earning an estimated $72.5 million from Friday through Sunday. This impressive haul secures the film's place as the second-best opening weekend of the year, trailing only behind *X-Men Origins: Wolverine*.

The film's success wasn't limited to traditional theaters. In premium large-format venues, *Star Trek* shattered box office history by setting a new one-weekend IMAX record, pulling in $8.2 million and decisively surpassing the previous benchmark of $6.3 million set by *The Dark Knight*. This achievement underscores the film's strong appeal in enhanced viewing formats, where audiences flocked to experience its space battles and visual spectacle on the largest screens available.

When factoring in an additional $4 million generated from Thursday night preview screenings, the film's total box office earnings climb to a remarkable $76.5 million. This figure significantly exceeds what many industry analysts had projected, signaling that Abrams' fresh take on the beloved sci-fi property has resonated with audiences far more strongly than anticipated.

Perhaps most tellingly, this opening weekend performance dwarfs every previous installment in the *Star Trek* cinematic franchise. For context, the next closest opening belongs to 1996's *Star Trek: First Contact*, which earned $30.7 million—meaning the new film's debut outperformed that milestone by well over double.

Adding to the promising outlook for the film's continued success, *Star Trek* earned a solid A grade on CinemaScore, a metric that measures audience satisfaction through opening-night polling. This strong grade suggests that positive word-of-mouth could play a crucial role in the weeks ahead, potentially helping the film expand its reach beyond the franchise's traditionally older, male-skewing fan base and attract a broader, more diverse audience to theaters.

# Star Trek Warps to Franchise-Best Opening Weekend

J.J. Abrams' bold reimagining of "Star Trek" has boldly gone where no entry in the franchise has gone before, rocketing to a massive $72.5 million opening weekend at the domestic box office. The number represents not only the biggest launch in the storied franchise's 40-plus year history, but also ranks as the second-highest opening of 2009 so far, trailing only behind Fox's "X-Men Origins: Wolverine."

The film's box office dominance was further amplified by its performance in premium large-format theaters, with IMAX screenings alone contributing a record-breaking $8.2 million—the best IMAX opening ever recorded. This exceptional showing in specialty theaters suggests that audiences were eager to experience Abrams' vision of the beloved sci-fi universe on the biggest screens possible, a testament to the film's sweeping visual scope and action-heavy sequences.

Critical reception has been overwhelmingly positive as well, with reviews praising Abrams for successfully revitalizing a franchise that had grown stale in the eyes of many casual moviegoers. This critical acclaim, combined with the film's strong technical execution, helped push the movie's total early earnings—factoring in Thursday night preview screenings and other early showings—to an impressive $76.5 million.

Perhaps most tellingly, "Star Trek" earned a rare A grade from CinemaScore, the market research firm that polls opening-night audiences on their satisfaction with a film. This grade is particularly significant because it indicates the movie resonated strongly with viewers beyond the built-in fanbase of hardcore Trekkies, who have historically skewed toward older male demographics. Industry analysts see this as a promising sign that "Star Trek" could enjoy strong word-of-mouth in the coming weeks, potentially expanding its audience to include younger viewers, women, and general moviegoers who might not otherwise have been drawn to a franchise reboot.

This broadening appeal could prove crucial for the film's long-term box office trajectory, as it will need to maintain momentum in the face of stiff competition from other major studio releases hitting theaters in the coming weeks. Chief among these rivals is "Angels & Demons," the highly anticipated sequel to "The Da Vinci Code" starring Tom Hanks, which is expected to draw significant crowds when it opens later this month. Whether "Star Trek" can hold its own against such heavyweight competition remains to be seen, but its strong debut, positive reviews, and audience satisfaction scores all point to a franchise that has successfully been relaunched for a new generation of fans.

# J.J. Abrams and Entertainment Weekly: A Hollywood Partnership

Entertainment Weekly, the American magazine dedicated to film, television, music, and popular culture, has long maintained a close relationship with the entertainment industry's most influential figures. Among these is J.J. Abrams, one of Hollywood's most versatile and successful creators, whose work has repeatedly captured the magazine's attention over the decades.

Since its founding in 1990, Entertainment Weekly has served as a chronicler of American pop culture, offering reviews, exclusive interviews, and behind-the-scenes coverage of major entertainment projects. J.J. Abrams, who first rose to prominence as a screenwriter before creating acclaimed television series like *Felicity*, *Alias*, and *Lost*, quickly became one of the magazine's favorite subjects. His ability to blend mystery, emotional storytelling, and mainstream appeal made him a natural fit for extensive editorial coverage.

The relationship between Abrams and Entertainment Weekly intensified as his career expanded into blockbuster filmmaking. When he took the helm of franchises like *Star Trek* and later *Star Wars: The Force Awakens*, the magazine provided in-depth coverage, including cover stories, set visits, and exclusive first-look images that generated significant buzz among fans. These features often highlighted Abrams' signature approach to storytelling—particularly his famous "mystery box" philosophy, which emphasizes withholding information to build anticipation and audience engagement.

Entertainment Weekly's coverage of Abrams also extended to his role as a producer, particularly through his production company, Bad Robot, which has been behind numerous television series and films that received substantial attention from the publication. The magazine's writers frequently analyzed his influence on shaping modern serialized television and event-driven cinema.

This ongoing coverage reflects a broader dynamic between entertainment journalism and prolific creators: publications like Entertainment Weekly rely on figures such as Abrams to generate reader interest, while creators benefit from the exposure and cultural conversation that such coverage generates. Together, they illustrate how media outlets and creative talents symbiotically shape the landscape of contemporary entertainment, keeping audiences informed and engaged with the evolving stories behind their favorite films and shows.

# 'Star Trek' Warps Past Competition in Blockbuster Debut

J.J. Abrams' bold reboot of *Star Trek* has boldly gone where no Trek film has gone before—straight to the top of the box office with the franchise's biggest opening ever.

The Paramount release beamed up an estimated $76.5 million in its first weekend, obliterating the previous franchise record held by 2002's *Star Trek: Nemesis* ($18.5 million) more than fourfold. In fact, this single opening weekend haul is inching close to what several previous Trek films earned in their *entire theatrical runs*. Even 1986's beloved *Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home*, adjusted for inflation, can't touch these numbers.

Credit the franchise's rejuvenation to Abrams' savvy strategy: cast rising stars (hello, Chris Pine and Zachary Quinto), bring back a beloved face for gravitas (Leonard Nimoy's Spock cameo has audiences verklempt), and market it as a sleek action thrill ride rather than a niche sci-fi property. The gamble paid off—early reports suggest a healthy 30% of the audience were women, and general moviegoers (not just Trekkies) turned out in droves, with CinemaScore reporting an A rating.

The victory is especially sweet coming one week after *X-Men Origins: Wolverine* clawed its way to a $85 million opening. While Wolverine still holds the edge in raw numbers, that film saw a steep 69% drop in its second weekend amid mixed reviews and an infamous workprint leak. *Star Trek*, by contrast, is boasting stellar reviews (95% on Rotten Tomatoes) and the kind of word-of-mouth that studios dream about, suggesting it may have significantly more staying power in the weeks ahead.

Rounding out the top five: *Wolverine* claimed second place with $26.2 million in its sophomore frame, followed by *Monsters vs. Aliens*, *Ghosts of Girlfriends Past*, and *Obsessed*.

With franchise-best numbers, critical acclaim, and a clear path forward (a sequel is already in the works), it seems the Enterprise crew has finally found the mainstream success that eluded them for over a decade. Somewhere, Gene Roddenberry is beaming with pride.
